newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Total, Unocal extend Burma ties despite protests.
newsitem.headline: Total, Unocal extend Burma ties despite protests.

text.p: Oil companies Total SA of France and Unocal Corp of the United States have extended ties with Burma despite increasing pressure from human rights activists protesting against the military rulers.
The two companies said on Thursday they had joined Burma's state-owned Myanmar Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) in a production sharing contract to explore an area in the Andaman Sea known as Block M8.
Unocal's vice-president for new ventures in South and Southeast Asia, John Vandermeer, was quoted in a Unocal press statement as saying: "We are happy to expand our opportunities in Myanmar (Burma)."

He said: "This step reflects Unocal's strategic focus on connecting growing energy markets to vitally needed energy resources. Increases in natural gas production can only bring broader growth to Myanmar's emerging economy."

But multinationals and particularly oil companies are coming under increasing pressure from human rights activists to withdraw from ventures with the military-ruled country, which has come under fire for suppressing moves towards democracy led by opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
Earlier this week human rights activists said they planned to step up protests against oil companies.
"The next focus is certainly the oil companies," said Larry Dohrs, spokesman for the Free Burma Coalition, which has headed a campaign to stop investment in Burma.
He was speaking after PepsiCo Inc followed a long line of international companies and said on Tuesday it had severed the last of its ties with Burma.

Unocal and Total have already come under pressure from the protesters, who said that other targets for their campaign would include Texaco Inc, which plans commercial production of natural gas off Burma in 1999, along with Nippon Oil Co Ltd.
Atlantic Richfield Co has a production sharing contract to drill on an offshore block in the Bay of Bangal.
A Unocal spokeswoman said the company did not believe sanctions would promote change.
"We believe that investment will speed economic growth and in turn will bring about change," she said by telephone from Burma.

Unocal and Total's major interest in Burma is the US$1.2 billion Yadana gas project, also in the Andaman Sea, which it shares with partners MOGE and Petroleum Authority of Thailand Exploration and Production

They expect to supply 525 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of natural gas to the Thai border through a 400-km (250-mile) pipeline. A further 125 mmcfd will be supplied to the domestic market in Burma. First production is expected in 1998.
The M8 deal involves surveying an area of 5,000 square km (4,275 square miles) of sea near the Yadana field for signs of oil or gas.
Unocal has taken a 47.5 percent stake and Total 52.5 percent. MOGE has a 15-percent option, which if exercised would cut the other partner's interests proportionately.

"In levels of investment, what M8 will add to (Yadana investment) is really very little," the Unocal spokeswoman said. Exploration is a process of constantly assessing whether results from surveys and then test wells show signs of enough oil and gas to justify further test drilling and eventually commercial production.
Surveying tends to be the cheapest stage of the process.

An official spokesman for Total was unavailable for comment. The head of the Asia division is now based in Paris following a company restructuring last year. Previously the company has said sanctions would not help development in the country.
In July Total rejected criticism it used forced or child labour in Burma. Both Unocal and Total have said they generally pay wages higher than those normally available in Burma.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
